t: #3858 Minimum Bitwise OR From Grid — Bit Greedy Over Row Feasibility
o: Pick one number per row minimizing their OR. Choices are independent per row, so a mask M is achievable as an upper bound iff every row contains some element that is a submask of M. Scan bits from high to low: tentatively set a bit and keep it if all rows still have a submask element. Example 2: [[3,5],[6,4]] — trying bit 2 fails (row 2 has no submask of 4), bit 1 succeeds with mask 5, giving 5.
k: OR of chosen values is a submask of M iff each chosen value individually is — rows are independent.
Greedy from the highest bit: keep a bit whenever feasibility (every row has a submask of the current mask) is preserved.

a.n: Approach 1: DP over achievable OR values
a.i: Maintain the set of OR values achievable using processed rows; extend it with each element of the next row. Intuitive and obviously correct; the set stays bounded by the number of distinct OR results in practice.
s: For each row, form nxt = { v | x : v in cur, x in row }.
After all rows, return the minimum of cur.
a.t: O(m * n * |S|) where |S| is the number of distinct achievable ORs (bounded by 2^18); usually fast, theoretically fragile.

a.i: Because row choices are independent, 'some selection has OR ⊆ M' reduces to 'every row has an element e with e & M == e'. Test each bit from high to low and commit it only if feasibility survives — this yields the minimum achievable OR.
s: For bit b from 17 down to 0: let m = ans | (1 << b).
If every row contains an element x with (x & m) == x, set ans = m.
a.t: O(B * m * n) with B = 18 bits — about 1.8e6 operations at the given limits.

w: Lead with the greedy in an interview; the independence-of-rows observation is the crux. Pitfall: testing 'row has an element equal to a submask' versus 'element that is a submask' — they are the same thing, but the check must be (x & m) == x, not (x & m) != 0. Follow-up: maximize the OR (same greedy keeping bits), or pick one element per row and per column.
